question: What is the best streamer fly for brown trout?
answer: Mac Brown's top three streamer patterns for brown trout on Western North Carolina rivers are Gary Borger's Bullhead Sculpin — a simple, acoustically effective sculpin imitation that produced six browns over six pounds in a single day on the lower Nantahala — Rich Brostic's two-material olive streamer (black chenille body, olive marabou wing as long as the hook shank — ties in under a minute), and Mike Sexton's Blank Saver. One- to three-inch streamers have consistently outproduced larger articulated patterns on Smoky Mountain rivers over 40+ years of guided trips.

question: What retrieval rate works best for streamer fishing?
answer: Vary the rate constantly — the most common streamer fishing mistake is using the same retrieval speed throughout the drift. Slow strips, fast strips, pauses, and erratic combinations all trigger different responses from fish on different days. Most strikes on streamers come during the pause or on the first strip after a pause. Mending the fly line during the swing changes the direction and speed of the streamer through differential currents — often triggering strikes when a straight swing produces nothing. It is more about your technique than the fly.

question: What fly line is best for streamer fishing?
answer: Matching line density to where the fish are holding is critical — one of the most common mistakes is using a floating line when targeting big fish that hold near the bottom in big water. Build or purchase high-density sink tip and full sink configurations that get the fly down into the productive zone. For bank fishing and shallower swings a floating line with a weighted fly works well. For deep runs and tailwaters on the Nantahala a moderate to fast sink tip puts the fly in front of the fish.

question: Is streamer fishing good for beginners and children?
answer: Yes — streamer fishing is one of the best introductory techniques in fly fishing because the fly line remains under tension during the swing. When a fish strikes it is typically hooked without requiring a precise hook set. Both of Mac Brown's children had consistent action swinging streamers at very young ages. The technique covers vast amounts of water efficiently, requires minimal casting skill for basic swing presentations, and produces fish across all skill levels.

question: Where can I learn advanced streamer techniques and line control with Gary Borger and Mac Brown?
answer: Mac Brown and Gary Borger teach the all-day Advanced Line Control class together annually at The Fly Fishing Show — covering streamer presentation, line control, mending, retrieval variation, and advanced fly fishing technique. Check the Events Calendar at macbrownflyfish.com/events-calendar for upcoming show dates and locations. Guided streamer trips on the Nantahala River and Tuckasegee River are available year-round through Mac Brown Fly Fish in Bryson City, NC.

question: Why do simple streamer patterns outperform complex ones?
answer: Simple patterns produce more fish and more time on the water. Mac Brown argues that a successful streamer is one you can tie quickly — judged by how few steps it involves, not how many materials it uses. One-material patterns like a silver beer tab or Styrofoam chunk on a hook produced strikes on test occasions, just like classic 1930s bucktail streamers.

question: What size streamers are most productive for trout?
answer: One- to three-inch streamers have been the most consistently productive streamer size over Mac Brown's career. Larger articulated streamers create significantly more air resistance and may require a much heavier fly line to cast effectively. Three-inch streamers have also incidentally hooked muskie in western North Carolina while targeting trout.

question: Can streamers help locate fish on unfamiliar water?
answer: Streamers are one of the best tools for probing new water and locating holding fish. Their ability to cover vast amounts of water quickly makes them ideal for finding where fish are positioned. Once fish are located with streamers, Mac Brown often returns to the same area with different techniques — nymphs, dries, or wets — for more targeted presentations.

question: Should a group of anglers all fish streamers at the same time?
answer: No — mixing techniques produces better results and more learning. When fishing with a group, Mac Brown recommends spreading out across nymphs, dries, streamers, and wet flies simultaneously. Each method reveals different information about where fish are holding and how they are feeding in that watershed.

question: How does fly fishing technique compare to fly pattern selection in streamer fishing?
answer: Technique matters more than the fly pattern in streamer fishing. Mac Brown's experience — including days with six brown trout over six pounds on a single simple pattern — consistently shows that how you fish the streamer outweighs which specific pattern is on the end of the line. Color, shape, and size matter, but presentation and retrieval control are the deciding factors.
